lead: A force on a rigid body can be moved anywhere along its own line of action without changing its external effect. The line of action is the infinite straight line along which the force acts; it passes through the point of application. This rule lets you redraw a free-body diagram with the force at a joint, corner or common point. It is used in beam and frame problems, in support reactions, and in reducing force systems. The rule is called the principle of transmissibility. It applies to the external effect on a rigid body, not to the internal forces inside it.
prereq: You need Unit 1: force as a vector and resolution of forces.

sections.h3: Line of action and the principle

blocks.text: A force is a vector: it has magnitude, direction and a point of application. Draw the force as an arrow from its point of application. The line of action is the infinite straight line along which the force acts. It passes through the point of application and runs in the direction of the force arrow. For a force of 100 N at A, the line of action passes through A and follows the arrow.

A rigid body is an ideal body whose points keep the same distance apart under load. No real body is perfectly rigid, but steel plates, beams and machine parts are treated as rigid for external reactions.

Principle of transmissibility: the external effect of a force on a rigid body is unchanged when the force is moved to any other point on its line of action, provided magnitude and direction stay the same. In vector language, forces on a rigid body are sliding vectors. Only three things count: magnitude, direction and line of action. The point of application on that line does not count.

Use 1: slide a force to a joint or corner. In a free-body diagram of a bracket, a cable force may act at a hole. For external reactions you may draw it at the pin centre if the line of action passes through both.

Use 2: slide forces to a common point before adding them. Two forces on a rigid body are slid along their own lines of action until they meet at the point where the two lines intersect. The two forces are then replaced by their vector sum acting at that intersection point (or by a resultant plus a couple if the lines are parallel). Only for collinear forces is the 'common line of action' language correct. This prepares the reduction of a force system in chapter 2.5. For moments, see chapter 2.2; a slide along the line keeps the perpendicular distance from any point O to the line unchanged, so the moment about O is unchanged.

Warning: the internal force changes. Slide a 100 N pull from one end of a rope to the other and the rope's internal tension distribution is not the same. The principle fails for deformable bodies such as ropes, springs and members you are checking for stress. It never allows turning the force, changing its magnitude, or moving it to a parallel line.

items: Draw the force arrow. Extend it to get the line of action.
Choose a new point on that same line, such as a joint or corner.
Redraw the same magnitude and direction at the new point.
Do not slide to a parallel line. That changes the line of action and the moment.

blocks.text: Check: The perpendicular distance from any moment centre to the line of action is unchanged by the slide, so M_O = F d is unchanged.

blocks.where: F is force in N; d is perpendicular distance from O to the line of action in m; M_O is moment about O in N·m.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this the principle of transmissibility of forces. The name comes from transmitting a force along its line. It is a modelling rule for external effects. It does not say the body is flexible or that every point feels the same force.

figure.caption: A 100 N force at A slides along its line of action to B. The pin reactions stay the same; the force is not turned or resized.

spec.title: Sliding a force on a rigid body
spec.aria: A force of 100 N applied at point A slides along its line of action to point B, and the reactions of the rigid body stay the same.

examples.question: A rigid plate is pinned at O. A force F = 100 N acts at point A on the plate. Its line of action passes at a perpendicular distance 0.4 m from O. The force is slid to point B on the same line of action; B is 1.2 m from O measured along the line of action. Find the moment of the force about O in both positions. State what happens to the pin reactions and to the internal force in the plate.
steps: Identify the line of action. Sliding from A to B keeps the same line.
The perpendicular distance from O to the line is d = 0.4 m in both positions. The 1.2 m is along the line, not perpendicular to it.
Moment magnitude is M_O = F d = 100 N × 0.4 m = 40 N·m.
The force tends to turn the plate the same way in both positions, so the moment vector is unchanged.
External pin reactions depend on the force's line, magnitude and direction, so they are unchanged. Internal force in the plate can change because the load path changes.
examples.answer: The moment about O is 40 N·m in both positions; pin reactions are unchanged, but the internal force in the plate is not.
examples.check:
F = 100.0
d = 0.4
M = F * d
print(M)

traps: Moving a force to a parallel line is not transmissibility. The line of action must be the same straight line.
The principle changes where the force is drawn, not its magnitude or direction.
External reactions may stay the same while internal forces and stresses change. Do not use the principle to find stress in a deformable member.
A force cannot be slid to a point that is not on its line of action just because it is convenient.
The distance used in M_O = F d is perpendicular to the line of action, not the distance along the line.

quiz.a: A force on a rigid body may be moved anywhere along its line of action without changing its external effect, if magnitude and direction stay the same.

quiz.q: Why does sliding a force along its line of action not change its moment about a point O?
quiz.a: The force magnitude and the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action stay the same, so M_O = F d is unchanged.

quiz.q: A force of 80 N acts on a rigid plate. Its line of action is 0.25 m from O. The force is slid 0.9 m along the line. Find the moment about O.
quiz.a: M_O = 80 N × 0.25 m = 20 N·m. The 0.9 m is along the line, so it does not enter the moment.

quiz.q: A truss member is loaded at a joint. Can you slide the force along its line to check the stress inside the member? Explain.
quiz.a: No for stress. The principle gives the same external reactions on a rigid body, but internal force and stress depend on where the load enters the member. Use the actual load position for stress.

quiz.q: What is the line of action of a force?
quiz.a: The infinite straight line along which the force acts; it passes through the point of application and runs in the direction of the force arrow.

quiz.q: Why are forces on a rigid body called sliding vectors?
quiz.a: Only magnitude, direction and line of action matter. The point of application may slide along that line without changing the external effect.

quiz.q: Two forces act on a rigid plate along the same line: 30 N one way and 50 N the other way. Slide them to a common point and find the resultant.
quiz.a: The vector sum is 50 N − 30 N = 20 N in the direction of the 50 N force.

quiz.q: A force is moved along its line on a rigid plate. The pin reactions do not change, but the internal force does. Explain both facts.
quiz.a: External equilibrium uses the force line, magnitude and direction, so reactions are unchanged. Internal force depends on the load path through the material, so it can change.

beyond: Not for the exam. In computer-aided design, loads are often moved to nodes or joints before a frame analysis; this is the same sliding-vector idea for external loads. Finite-element software keeps the actual load distribution when stresses matter, because transmissibility is not valid inside a deformable body. Search for 'sliding vector', 'equivalent nodal loads' and 'Saint-Venant principle' to see how load placement is handled in design. The safe habit is to slide for reactions, but not for stress.
